claim: Hsp104 is composed of a N-terminal domain (NTD), nucleotide-binding domain 1 (NBD1), middle domain (MD), nucleotide-binding domain 2 (NBD2), and C-terminal domain (CTD).
source: Hsp104 is composed of a N-terminal domain (NTD), nucleotide-binding domain 1 (NBD1), middle domain (MD), nucleotide-binding domain 2 (NBD2), and C-terminal domain (CTD).
evidence: This is stated directly in the figure legend describing the domain structure of Hsp104.

claim: Hsp78 is composed of a mitochondrial-targeting signal (MTS), NBD1, MD, NBD2, and CTD.
source: Hsp78 is composed of a mitochondrial-targeting signal (MTS), NBD1, MD, NBD2, and CTD.
evidence: This is stated directly in the figure legend describing the domain structure of Hsp78.

claim: Skd3 is composed of a MTS, a short hydrophobic stretch of unknown function, an ankyrin-repeat domain (ANK) containing four ankyrin repeats, an NBD that is homologous to Hsp104 and Hsp78 NBD2, and a CTD.
source: Skd3 is composed of a MTS, a short hydrophobic stretch of unknown function, an ankyrin-repeat domain (ANK) containing four ankyrin repeats, an NBD that is homologous to Hsp104 and Hsp78 NBD2, and a CTD.
evidence: This is stated directly in the figure legend describing the domain structure of Skd3.

claim: Skd3 is conserved across diverse metazoan species.
source: The alignment shows conservation of Skd3 across diverse species and shows high similarity between mammalian Skd3 proteins.
evidence: The phylogenetic tree in Figure 1B and the accompanying text demonstrate conservation across species.

claim: Protein aggregation and aberrant phase transitions are elicited by a variety of cellular stressors and can be highly toxic.
source: Protein aggregation and aberrant phase transitions are elicited by a variety of cellular stressors and can be highly toxic (Chuang et al., 2018; Eisele et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Cells have evolved specialized protein disaggregases to reverse aggregation and restore resolubilized proteins to native structure and function.
source: To counter this challenge, cells have evolved specialized protein disaggregases to reverse aggregation and restore resolubilized proteins to native structure and function (Shorter, 2017; Shorter and Southworth, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Protein disaggregases are conserved across all domains of life, with orthologues of Hsp104 powering protein disaggregation and reactivation in eubacteria and nonmetazoan eukaryotes.
source: Indeed, protein disaggregases are conserved across all domains of life, with orthologues of Hsp104, a ring-shaped hexameric AAA+ protein, powering protein disaggregation and reactivation (as opposed to degradation) in eubacteria and nonmetazoan eukaryotes (Glover and Lindquist, 1998; Goloubinoff et al., 1999; Queitsch et al., 2000; Shorter, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: In nonmetazoan eukaryotes, Hsp104 functions in the cytoplasm and nucleus.
source: In nonmetazoan eukaryotes, Hsp104 functions in the cytoplasm and nucleus (Parsell et al., 1994; Tkach and Glover, 2008; Wallace et al., 2015), whereas the closely-related AAA+ disaggregase, Hsp78, resolubilizes and reactivates proteins in mitochondria (Krzewska et al., 2001; Schmitt et al., 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Hsp78 resolubilizes and reactivates proteins in mitochondria.
source: In nonmetazoan eukaryotes, Hsp104 functions in the cytoplasm and nucleus (Parsell et al., 1994; Tkach and Glover, 2008; Wallace et al., 2015), whereas the closely-related AAA+ disaggregase, Hsp78, resolubilizes and reactivates proteins in mitochondria (Krzewska et al., 2001; Schmitt et al., 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: At the evolutionary transition from protozoa to metazoa both Hsp104 and Hsp78 are lost and are subsequently absent from all animal species.
source: Curiously, at the evolutionary transition from protozoa to metazoa both Hsp104 and Hsp78 are lost and are subsequently absent from all animal species (Erives and Fassler, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The loss of Hsp104 and Hsp78 is perplexing given that toxic protein aggregation remains a major challenge in metazoa.
source: This loss of Hsp104 and Hsp78 is perplexing given that toxic protein aggregation remains a major challenge in metazoa (Eisele et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and represents an inference about the evolutionary puzzle.

claim: Ectopic expression of Hsp104 is well tolerated by animal cells and can be neuroprotective in animal models of neurodegenerative disease.
source: Indeed, it is even more baffling since ectopic expression of Hsp104 is well tolerated by animal cells and can be neuroprotective in animal models of neurodegenerative disease (Cushman-Nick et al., 2013; Dandoy-Dron et al., 2006; Jackrel et al., 2014; Lo Bianco et al., 2008; Perrin et al., 2007; Satyal et al., 2000; Vacher et al., 2005; Yasuda et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Metazoa may partially compensate for the absence of Hsp104 activity in the cytoplasm and nucleus with alternative general protein-disaggregase systems, such as Hsp110, Hsp70, Hsp40, and small heat-shock proteins.
source: Metazoa may partially compensate for the absence of Hsp104 activity in the cytoplasm and nucleus with alternative general protein-disaggregase systems, such as Hsp110, Hsp70, Hsp40, and small heat-shock proteins (Duennwald et al., 2012; Mattoo et al., 2013; Nillegoda et al., 2015; Scior et al., 2018; Shorter, 2011; Shorter, 2017; Torrente and Shorter, 2013) as well as client-specific disaggregases in the cytoplasm such as nuclear-import receptors (Guo et al., 2019; Guo et al., 2018; Niaki et al., 2020; Yoshizawa et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Hsp110 is not found in mitochondria.
source: However, Hsp110 is not found in mitochondria (Voos and Röttgers, 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: It continues to remain uncertain whether, in the absence of Hsp78, metazoan mitochondria harbor a disaggregase that solubilizes and reactivates aggregated proteins.
source: Thus, it continues to remain uncertain whether, in the absence of Hsp78, metazoan mitochondria harbor a disaggregase that solubilizes and reactivates aggregated proteins.
evidence: This statement represents the knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: Skd3 is a ubiquitously expressed, mitochondrial AAA+ protein of poorly-defined function.
source: Skd3 is a ubiquitously expressed, mitochondrial AAA+ protein of poorly-defined function, which is related to Hsp104 and Hsp78 via its HCLR clade AAA+ domain (Figure 1a and Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Erzberger and Berger, 2006; Périer et al., 1995; Seraphim and Houry, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Skd3 is related to Hsp104 and Hsp78 via its HCLR clade AAA+ domain.
source: Skd3 is a ubiquitously expressed, mitochondrial AAA+ protein of poorly-defined function, which is related to Hsp104 and Hsp78 via its HCLR clade AAA+ domain (Figure 1a and Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Erzberger and Berger, 2006; Périer et al., 1995; Seraphim and Houry, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Skd3 appears to play an important role in maintaining mitochondrial structure and function.
source: Skd3 appears to play an important role in maintaining mitochondrial structure and function (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Skd3 first appears in evolution alongside Hsp104 and Hsp78 in choanoflagellates.
source: Curiously, Skd3 first appears in evolution alongside Hsp104 and Hsp78 in choanoflagellates, a group of free-living unicellular and colonial flagellate eukaryotes that are the closest extant protozoan relatives of animals (Figure 1b and Supplementary file 1; Brunet and King, 2017; Erives and Fassler, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: During the complex evolutionary transition from protozoa to metazoa, Skd3 is retained, whereas Hsp104 and Hsp78 are lost.
source: During the complex evolutionary transition from protozoa to metazoa, Skd3 is retained, whereas Hsp104 and Hsp78 are lost (Erives and Fassler, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Skd3 is conserved in many metazoan lineages.
source: Indeed, Skd3 is conserved in many metazoan lineages (Figure 1a,b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and Supplementary file 1; Erives and Fassler, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and figures showing phylogenetic conservation.

claim: The Skd3 NBD closely resembles NBD2 of Hsp104 and Hsp78.
source: The Skd3 NBD closely resembles NBD2 of Hsp104 and Hsp78 (Figure 1a and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by figures showing domain alignments.

claim: Aside from the NBD similarity, Skd3 is highly divergent from Hsp104 and Hsp78.
source: Aside from this similarity, Skd3 is highly divergent from Hsp104 and Hsp78 (Figure 1a and Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Torrente and Shorter, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and figures showing domain comparisons.

claim: The Skd3 CTD is basic compared to the more acidic Hsp104 and Hsp78 CTDs.
source: For example, Skd3, Hsp104, and Hsp78 all have short CTDs, but these are divergent with the Skd3 CTD being basic compared to the more acidic Hsp104 and Hsp78 CTDs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to a figure showing sequence alignments.

claim: The other domains in Hsp104 (NTD, NBD1, and MD) and Hsp78 (NBD1 and MD) are not found in Skd3.
source: Moreover, the other domains in Hsp104 (N-terminal domain [NTD], NBD1, and middle domain [MD]) and Hsp78 (NBD1 and MD) are not found in Skd3 (Figure 1a and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by figures showing domain structures.

claim: The ankyrin-repeat domain is an important substrate-binding domain of chloroplast signal recognition particle 43 (cpSRP43).
source: In their place, is an ankyrin-repeat domain (Figure 1a), which interestingly is an important substrate-binding domain of another protein disaggregase, chloroplast signal recognition particle 43 (cpSRP43) (Jaru-Ampornpan et al., 2013; Jaru-Ampornpan et al., 2010; McAvoy et al., 2018; Nguyen et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Mutations in the Skd3 ankyrin-repeat domain and NBD are linked to 3-methylglutaconic aciduria, type VII (MGCA7).
source: Importantly, mutations in the Skd3 ankyrin-repeat domain and NBD are linked to the rare, but severe mitochondrial disorder, 3-methylglutaconic aciduria, type VII (MGCA7) (Capo-Chichi et al., 2015; Kanabus et al., 2015; Kiykim et al., 2016; Pronicka et al., 2017; Saunders et al., 2015; Wortmann et al., 2016; Wortmann et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: MGCA7 is an autosomal recessive metabolic disorder that presents with increased levels of 3-methylglutaconic acid (3-MGA), neurologic deterioration, and neutropenia.
source: MGCA7 is an autosomal recessive metabolic disorder that presents with increased levels of 3-methylglutaconic acid (3-MGA), neurologic deterioration, and neutropenia (Wortmann et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Patients with MGCA7 typically present with infantile onset of a progressive encephalopathy with movement abnormalities and delayed psychomotor development.
source: Typically, patients present with infantile onset of a progressive encephalopathy with movement abnormalities and delayed psychomotor development (Wortmann et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Common but variable phenotypes of MGCA7 include cataracts, seizures, and recurrent infections.
source: Other common, but variable, phenotypes include cataracts, seizures, and recurrent infections (Wortmann et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Severe MGCA7 can result in afflicted infants typically only living for a few weeks or months.
source: These issues can be severe with afflicted infants typically only living for a few weeks or months (Wortmann et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Patients with moderate MGCA7 may present with neutropenia, hypotonia, spasticity, movement abnormalities, epilepsy, and intellectual disability.
source: Patients may also present with more moderate phenotypes, including neutropenia, hypotonia, spasticity, movement abnormalities, epilepsy, and intellectual disability (Wortmann et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Mildly affected MGCA7 individuals have no neurological problems, normal life expectancy, but present with neutropenia.
source: Mildly affected individuals have no neurological problems, normal life expectancy, but present with neutropenia (Wortmann et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: There is no cure and no effective therapeutics for severe or moderate forms of MGCA7.
source: There is no cure and no effective therapeutics for severe or moderate forms of MGCA7.
evidence: This statement represents current knowledge about the disease.

claim: Little is known about how Skd3 mutations might cause MGCA7.
source: Moreover, little is known about how Skd3 mutations might cause disease.
evidence: This statement represents the knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: MPPSkd3 displayed robust ATPase activity that was comparable to Hsp104.
source: Indeed, MPPSkd3 displayed robust ATPase activity that was comparable to Hsp104 and over two-fold higher than previously reported values for MPPSkd3 activity (Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 2a; Mróz et al., 2020; Wortmann et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: MPPSkd3 ATPase activity was over two-fold higher than previously reported values.
source: Indeed, MPPSkd3 displayed robust ATPase activity that was comparable to Hsp104 and over two-fold higher than previously reported values for MPPSkd3 activity (Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 2a; Mróz et al., 2020; Wortmann et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data and comparison to cited literature.

claim: Hsp70 and Hsp40 were unable to recover any active luciferase and were similar to the buffer control.
source: Indeed, Hsp70 and Hsp40 were unable to recover any active luciferase (~0.05 ± 0.00% [mean ± SEM] native luciferase activity) and were similar to the buffer control (~0.04 ± 0.00% native luciferase activity) (Figure 2c and Figure 2—figure supplement 2b,d).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Hsp104 alone was unable to disaggregate and reactivate luciferase.
source: As expected, Hsp104 alone was also unable to disaggregate and reactivate luciferase (~0.08 ± 0.01% native luciferase activity) (Figure 2c and Figure 2—figure supplement 2b,d; DeSantis et al., 2012; Glover and Lindquist, 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data and citations to published literature.

claim: The combination of Hsp104, Hsp70, and Hsp40 recovered approximately 7.68% native luciferase activity.
source: By contrast, the combination of Hsp104, Hsp70, and Hsp40 recovered ~7.68 ± 0.44% native luciferase activity (Figure 2c and Figure 2—figure supplement 2b,d; Glover and Lindquist, 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: MPPSkd3 displayed robust disaggregase activity in the presence of ATP as it was able to recover approximately 2.87% native luciferase activity.
source: Remarkably, MPPSkd3 displayed robust disaggregase activity in the presence of ATP as it was able to recover ~2.87 ± 0.17% native luciferase activity (Figure 2c and Figure 2—figure supplement 2b,c).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: MPPSkd3 displayed approximately 40% of the disaggregase activity of Hsp104 plus Hsp70 and Hsp40.
source: Indeed, MPPSkd3 displayed ~40% of the disaggregase activity of Hsp104 plus Hsp70 and Hsp40 under these conditions (Figure 2c).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: MPPSkd3 had no requirement for Hsp70 and Hsp40 for disaggregase activity.
source: While Hsp104 required the presence of Hsp70 and Hsp40 to disaggregate luciferase (Figure 2c and Figure 2—figure supplement 2b,c; DeSantis et al., 2012; Glover and Lindquist, 1998), MPPSkd3 had no requirement for Hsp70 and Hsp40 (Figure 2c and Figure 2—figure supplement 2b,c).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: MPPSkd3 is a 'stand-alone' disaggregase.
source: This finding indicates that MPPSkd3 is a 'stand-alone' disaggregase.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that MPPSkd3 does not require Hsp70 and Hsp40.

claim: MPPSkd3 disaggregase activity was supported by ATP but not by the absence of nucleotide or the presence of ADP.
source: MPPSkd3 disaggregase activity was supported by ATP but not by the absence of nucleotide or the presence of ADP (Figure 2c and Figure 2—figure supplement 2b,d).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Neither the non-hydrolyzable ATP analogue, AMP-PNP, nor the slowly hydrolyzable ATP analogue, ATPγS, could support MPPSkd3 disaggregase activity.
source: Likewise, neither the non-hydrolyzable ATP analogue, AMP-PNP, nor the slowly hydrolyzable ATP analogue, ATPγS, could support MPPSkd3 disaggregase activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 2b,d).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: MPPSkd3 disaggregase activity requires multiple rounds of rapid ATP binding and hydrolysis.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that MPPSkd3 disaggregase activity requires multiple rounds of rapid ATP binding and hydrolysis, which is similar mechanistically to Hsp104 (DeSantis et al., 2012; Shorter and Lindquist, 2004; Shorter and Lindquist, 2006).
evidence: This is an inference based on the nucleotide requirements and comparison to Hsp104.

claim: MPPSkd3K387A (Walker A mutant) and MPPSkd3E455Q (Walker B mutant) displayed greatly reduced ATPase and disaggregase activity.
source: Likewise, MPPSkd3K387A (Walker A mutant) and MPPSkd3E455Q (Walker B mutant) displayed greatly reduced ATPase and disaggregase activity (Figure 2d,e).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d,e.

claim: MPPSkd3 couples ATP binding and hydrolysis to protein disaggregation.
source: Thus, MPPSkd3 couples ATP binding and hydrolysis to protein disaggregation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the effects of Walker A and Walker B mutations.

claim: The pore-loop variant, MPPSkd3Y430A, exhibited reduced ATPase activity compared to MPPSkd3.
source: Interestingly, the pore-loop variant, MPPSkd3Y430A, exhibited reduced ATPase activity compared to MPPSkd3, but much higher ATPase activity than MPPSkd3K387A and MPPSkd3E455Q (Figure 2d).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: MPPSkd3Y430A was devoid of disaggregase activity.
source: MPPSkd3Y430A was also devoid of disaggregase activity (Figure 2e).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: The pore-loop Y430 might make direct contact with substrate to drive protein disaggregation.
source: The inhibition of disaggregase activity by Y430A was much more severe than the inhibition of ATPase activity (Figure 2d,e), which suggests that the pore-loop Y430 might make direct contact with substrate to drive protein disaggregation as in Hsp104 (DeSantis et al., 2012; Gates et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects on ATPase and disaggregase activity.

claim: The conserved putative substrate-binding tyrosine of the -GYVG- pore-loop is critical for MPPSkd3 disaggregase activity.
source: Thus, the conserved putative substrate-binding tyrosine of the -GYVG- pore-loop is critical for MPPSkd3 disaggregase activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the effects of the Y430A mutation.

claim: Skd3 is cleaved by the inner-membrane rhomboid protease, PARL, at amino acid 127.
source: Intriguingly, Skd3 is cleaved by the inner-membrane rhomboid protease, PARL, at amino acid 127, between the 35-amino acid, hydrophobic stretch and the ankyrin-repeat domain (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Saita et al., 2017; Spinazzi et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The 35-amino acid, hydrophobic stretch and the PARL-cleavage motif are both highly conserved among mammalian Skd3 orthologues.
source: Sequence analysis shows that the 35-amino acid, hydrophobic stretch and the PARL-cleavage motif are both highly conserved among mammalian Skd3 orthologues (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This statement is supported by sequence analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2a.

claim: The absence of the 35-residue stretch that is removed by PARL slightly decreased Skd3 ATPase activity compared to MPPSkd3.
source: We found that the absence of the 35-residue stretch that is removed by PARL slightly decreased Skd3 ATPase activity compared to MPPSkd3 (Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: MPPSkd3 ATPase activity is not stimulated by the model substrate, casein.
source: Moreover, we find that MPPSkd3 ATPase activity is not stimulated by the model substrate, casein, a classic peptide-stimulator of Hsp104 ATPase activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 3; Cashikar et al., 2002; Gates et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: PARLSkd3 ATPase activity is mildly stimulated by casein.
source: By contrast, PARLSkd3 ATPase activity is mildly stimulated by casein (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: PARLSkd3 may interact more effectively with substrates than MPPSkd3 due to the removal of the 35-amino acid, hydrophobic stretch.
source: This finding indicates that PARLSkd3 may interact more effectively with substrates than MPPSkd3 due to the removal of the 35-amino acid, hydrophobic stretch.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential casein stimulation.

claim: PARLSkd3 exhibited over 10-fold higher disaggregase activity compared to MPPSkd3.
source: Remarkably, the absence of the N-terminal peptide known to be removed by PARL unleashed Skd3 disaggregase activity (Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 2c,d). Indeed, PARLSkd3 exhibited over 10-fold higher disaggregase activity (~44.06 ± 3.78% native luciferase activity recovered, mean ± SEM) compared to MPPSkd3 (~3.10 ± 0.44% native luciferase activity recovered) and over five-fold higher disaggregation activity than Hsp104 plus Hsp70 and Hsp40 (~8.58 ± 1.20% native luciferase activity recovered), despite PARLSkd3 having lower ATPase activity when compared to MPPSkd3 (Figure 3b,c, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2b,c,d).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: PARLSkd3 exhibited over five-fold higher disaggregation activity than Hsp104 plus Hsp70 and Hsp40.
source: Remarkably, the absence of the N-terminal peptide known to be removed by PARL unleashed Skd3 disaggregase activity (Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 2c,d). Indeed, PARLSkd3 exhibited over 10-fold higher disaggregase activity (~44.06 ± 3.78% native luciferase activity recovered, mean ± SEM) compared to MPPSkd3 (~3.10 ± 0.44% native luciferase activity recovered) and over five-fold higher disaggregation activity than Hsp104 plus Hsp70 and Hsp40 (~8.58 ± 1.20% native luciferase activity recovered), despite PARLSkd3 having lower ATPase activity when compared to MPPSkd3 (Figure 3b,c, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2b,c,d).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Skd3 disaggregase activity is likely regulated by PARL.
source: These results suggest that Skd3 disaggregase activity is likely regulated by PARL and that PARL-activated Skd3 is a powerful, stand-alone protein disaggregase with activity comparable to potentiated Hsp104 variants (Jackrel et al., 2014; Jackrel and Shorter, 2014; Jackrel et al., 2015; Tariq et al., 2019; Tariq et al., 2018; Torrente et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on the dramatic increase in activity after PARL cleavage.

claim: PARL-activated Skd3 is a powerful, stand-alone protein disaggregase with activity comparable to potentiated Hsp104 variants.
source: These results suggest that Skd3 disaggregase activity is likely regulated by PARL and that PARL-activated Skd3 is a powerful, stand-alone protein disaggregase with activity comparable to potentiated Hsp104 variants (Jackrel et al., 2014; Jackrel and Shorter, 2014; Jackrel et al., 2015; Tariq et al., 2019; Tariq et al., 2018; Torrente et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on the high disaggregase activity and comparison to cited literature.

claim: PARLSkd3 disaggregase activity was supported by ATP, but not in the absence of nucleotide or in the presence of ADP, non-hydrolyzable AMP-PNP, or slowly hydrolyzable ATPγS.
source: As with MPPSkd3, we found that PARLSkd3 disaggregase activity was supported by ATP, but not in the absence of nucleotide or in the presence of ADP, non-hydrolyzable AMP-PNP, or slowly hydrolyzable ATPγS (Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 2e).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 2e.

claim: PARLSkd3K387A (Walker A mutant) and PARLSkd3E455Q (Walker B mutant) lacked ATPase and disaggregase activity.
source: Likewise, PARLSkd3K387A (Walker A mutant) and PARLSkd3E455Q (Walker B mutant) lacked ATPase and disaggregase activity (Figure 3d,e), indicating that PARLSkd3 couples ATP binding and hydrolysis to protein disaggregation.
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3d,e.

claim: PARLSkd3 couples ATP binding and hydrolysis to protein disaggregation.
source: Likewise, PARLSkd3K387A (Walker A mutant) and PARLSkd3E455Q (Walker B mutant) lacked ATPase and disaggregase activity (Figure 3d,e), indicating that PARLSkd3 couples ATP binding and hydrolysis to protein disaggregation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the effects of Walker A and Walker B mutations.

claim: PARLSkd3Y430A (pore-loop mutant) exhibited a larger reduction in ATPase activity than MPPSkd3Y430A.
source: Curiously, PARLSkd3Y430A (pore-loop mutant) exhibited a larger reduction in ATPase activity than MPPSkd3Y430A (Figures 2d and 3d), indicating that the conserved tyrosine in the conserved putative substrate-binding -GYVG- pore loop impacts ATPase activity in Skd3, whereas it has no effect in Hsp104 (DeSantis et al., 2012; Torrente et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2d and 3d.

claim: PARLSkd3Y430A was devoid of disaggregase activity.
source: PARLSkd3Y430A was devoid of disaggregase activity (Figure 3e), which could be due to reduced ATPase activity, reduced substrate binding, or both.
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: PARLSkd3, but not MPPSkd3, disaggregated disease-causing α-synuclein fibrils in the presence, but not absence of ATP.
source: Using a sedimentation assay combined with a dot-blot, we found that PARLSkd3, but not MPPSkd3 (data not shown), disaggregated these disease-causing fibrils in the presence, but not absence of ATP (Figure 4a,b).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a,b.

claim: PARLSkd3 is a powerful protein disaggregase, which could have applications as a potential therapeutic agent to eliminate disease-causing α-synuclein fibrils that underlie Parkinson's disease and other synucleinopathies.
source: Thus, PARLSkd3 is a powerful protein disaggregase, which could have applications as a potential therapeutic agent to eliminate disease-causing α-synuclein fibrils that underlie Parkinson's disease and other synucleinopathies.
evidence: This is speculation based on the ability to disaggregate α-synuclein fibrils.

claim: Neither the isolated ankyrin-repeat domain nor the isolated NBD exhibited ATPase activity or disaggregase activity.
source: Neither the isolated ankyrin-repeat domain nor the isolated NBD exhibited ATPase activity or disaggregase activity (Figure 5b,c).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5b,c.

claim: The ankyrin-repeat domain and NBD combine in cis to enable Skd3 ATPase activity and disaggregase activity.
source: Thus, the ankyrin-repeat domain and NBD combine in cis to enable Skd3 ATPase activity and disaggregase activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of activity of isolated domains.

claim: Equimolar amounts of the ankyrin-repeat domain and NBD were inactive when combined in trans.
source: We also tested whether the two domains could combine in trans as two separate proteins to yield an active ATPase or disaggregase. However, we found that equimolar amounts of the ankyrin-repeat domain and NBD were also inactive (Figure 5b,c).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5b,c.

claim: The covalent linkage of the ankyrin-repeat domain and NBD is critical for forming a functional ATPase and disaggregase.
source: These findings suggest that the covalent linkage of the ankyrin-repeat domain and NBD is critical for forming a functional ATPase and disaggregase.
evidence: This is an inference based on the inability of separate domains to reconstitute activity.

claim: Truncated MGCA7-linked Skd3 variants, such as R250* and K321*, which lack the NBD would be inactive for protein disaggregation and any ATPase-dependent activities.
source: Importantly, they also predict that truncated MGCA7-linked Skd3 variants, such as R250* and K321* (where * indicates a stop codon), which lack the NBD would be inactive for protein disaggregation and indeed any ATPase-dependent activities.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the requirement for both domains.

claim: Neither MPPSkd3 nor PARLSkd3 disaggregase activity was stimulated by Hsp70 and Hsp40.
source: Thus, we tested if Hsp70 and Hsp40 could stimulate Skd3 disaggregase activity. However, neither MPPSkd3 nor PARLSkd3disaggregase activity was stimulated by Hsp70 and Hsp40 (Figure 6a,b).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6a,b.

claim: Skd3 is a stand-alone disaggregase that works independently of the Hsp70 chaperone system.
source: Thus, Skd3 is a stand-alone disaggregase that works independently of the Hsp70 chaperone system.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of stimulation by Hsp70 and Hsp40.

claim: Human cells lacking Skd3 exhibit decreased protein solubility in mitochondria.
source: Overall, we observed decreased protein solubility in mitochondria from the Skd3 knockout cells when compared to their wild-type counterparts (Figure 7b and Figure 7—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This statement is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 7b.
